हिमाचल में कहीं 0 पर लुढ़का पारा, कहीं 32 डिग्री तापमान, पहाड़ों पर सर्दी, मैदान गर्मी से बेहाल
मौसम विभाग ने हिमाचल प्रदेश में आगामी दिनों के लिए पूर्वानुमान जारी किया है, फिलहाल प्रदेश में न्यूनतम तापमान बढ़ सकता है.
शिमला: हिमाचल प्रदेश में कुछ दिनों से मौसम शुष्क और साफ बना हुआ है. हालांकि बीते दिनों हुई बारिश-बर्फबारी के चलते प्रदेश में अक्टूबर महीने में ही सर्दियों की एंट्री हो गई है. ऐसे में हिमाचल में मौसम के अलग-अलग रंग देखने को मिल रहे हैं. जहां पहाड़ों पर पारा शून्य तक लुढ़क गया है. वहीं, निचले व मैदानी इलाके गर्मी से बेहाल हो रहे हैं और पारा 32.0 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिकतम तापमान तक पहुंच गया है.
कहीं ठंड तो कहीं गर्मी का मौसम
मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक, ताबो में सबसे कम 0.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस न्यूनतम तापमान, जबकि ऊना में सबसे ज्यादा 32.0 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिकतम तापमान दर्ज किया गया है. ऊंचे पहाड़ी इलाकों में न्यूनतम तापमान 0 से 10 °C, मध्यम पहाड़ी इलाकों में 6 से 17 °C और निचले इलाकों में 11 से 19 °C दर्ज किया गया है. वहीं, बात करें अधिकतम तापमान की तो ऊंचाई वाले इलाकों में 15 से 20 °C, मध्य पर्वतीय इलाकों में 21 से 29 °C और निचले व मैदानी इलाकों में 27 से 32 °C के बीच रहा.
अगले 24 घंटे तक बढ़ेगा तापमान
मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र शिमला के अनुसार मौसम साफ रहने के चलते अगले 24 घंटे तक प्रदेश में कई हिस्सों में न्यूनतम तापमान 2 से 3 °C तक बढ़ने की संभावना है. इसके बाद अगले 2-3 दिनों में प्रदेश के कई हिस्सों में न्यूनतम तापमान 2-4 °C तक गिर सकता है और इस दौरान अधिकतम तापमान में भी 2-5 °C तक गिरावट दर्ज की जा सकती है. 24 अक्टूबर को प्रदेश में नए पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के सक्रिय होने की संभावना है.
प्रदेश में कब होगी बारिश-बर्फबारी ?
ऐसे में 24 अक्टूबर से मौसम फिर से करवट लेने वाला है और दो दिन प्रदेश के कई हिस्सों में हल्की बारिश-बर्फबारी होने की संभावना है. मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र शिमला के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, 24 अक्टूबर को चंबा, कांगड़ा, कुल्लू, मंडी, शिमला, किन्नौर और लाहौल-स्पीति में हल्की बारिश-बर्फबारी हो सकती है. वहीं, 25 अक्टूबर को चंबा, कांगड़ा, कुल्लू, किन्नौर और लाहौल-स्पीति में हल्की बारिश-बर्फबारी होने की संभावना है.
प्रदेश में न्यूनतम तापमान
प्रदेश में सबसे कम 0.1 °C न्यूनतम तापमान ताबो में दर्ज किया गया. इसके अलावा शिमला में 12.0 °C, सुंदरनगर में 9.4, भुंतर में 8.4, कल्पा में 4.2, धर्मशाला में 14.6, ऊना में 13.0, नाहन में 14.6, केलांग में 0.5, पालमपुर में 10.2, सोलन में 8.5, मनाली में 6.4, कांगड़ा में 13.0, मंडी में 11.1, बिलासपुर में 12.0, चंबा में 10.5, जुब्बड़हट्टी में 13.0, कुफरी में 10.4, कुकुमसेरी में 0.8, भरमौर में 12.0, सेउबाग में 7.3, बरठीं में 12.2, पांवटा साहिब में 19.0, सराहन में 17.2, देहरा गोपीपुर में 15.0, नेरी में 15.6 और बजौरा में 7.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस न्यूनतम तापमान दर्ज किया गया.
हिमाचल में अधिकतम तापमान
हिमाचल में ऊना 32.0 °C अधिकतम तापमान के साथ सबसे गर्म रहा. वहीं, शिमला में 22.2 °C, सुंदरनगर में 28.9, भुंतर में 28.8, कल्पा में 19.2, धर्मशाला में 26.0, नाहन में 24.9, केलांग में 15.4, पालमपुर में 24.4, सोलन में 25.4, मनाली में 21.0, कांगड़ा में 28.7, मंडी में 28.2, बिलासपुर में 28.0, चंबा में 26.4, जुब्बड़हट्टी में 24.2, कुफरी में 16.1, बरठीं में 28.8, ताबो में 17.3, नेरी में 29.2 और बजौरा में 28.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिकतम तापमान दर्ज किया गया.

चंडीगढ़:हरियाणा में मौसम एक बार फिर करवट लेने जा रहा है. 24 अक्टूबर की देर रात से प्रदेश के कई हिस्सों में बूंदाबांदी होने की संभावना है. मौसम विभाग के अनुसार आंशिक प्रभाव वाले पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के कारण 25 और 26 अक्टूबर को मौसम में बदलाव देखने को मिल सकता है.
पश्चिमी विक्षोभ से बदलेगी हवाओं की दिशा:मौसम वैज्ञानिकों के मुताबिक पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के आंशिक प्रभाव से प्रदेश में हवाओं का रुख उत्तर-पश्चिमी से बदलकर उत्तर-पूर्वी होने की संभावना है. इसके चलते कई जिलों में गरज-चमक के साथ छिटपुट बूंदाबांदी या हल्की बारिश हो सकती है. मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक 25 और 26 अक्टूबर को मौसम आमतौर पर परिवर्तनशील रहेगा. 26 अक्टूबर के बाद प्रदेश में मौसम दोबारा शुष्क होने की संभावना है.
दिन में गिरेगा तापमान:मौसम में बदलाव के दौरान दिन के तापमान में हल्की गिरावट आने का अनुमान है. इससे सुबह और शाम के समय ठंड का अहसास बढ़ सकता है. वहीं, बादलों की आवाजाही के कारण रात के न्यूनतम तापमान में मामूली बढ़ोतरी होने की संभावना जताई गई है. ऐसे में दिन और रात के तापमान में अंतर देखने को मिल सकता है.
गुरुग्राम 33.8 डिग्री के साथ सबसे गर्म:वहीं, प्रदेश में अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य के आसपास बना हुआ है. उपलब्ध मौसम आंकड़ों के अनुसार गुरुग्राम में सबसे अधिक 33.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान दर्ज किया गया. नूंह में 33.5 डिग्री, हिसार, चरखी दादरी और फरीदाबाद में 33.1-33.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान रहा. वहीं, पंचकूला में अधिकतम तापमान सबसे कम 29.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया.
गुरुग्राम में रात का पारा 14 डिग्री:इसके साथ ही न्यूनतम तापमान के आंकड़ों में जिलों के बीच बड़ा अंतर देखने को मिला. गुरुग्राम में रात का तापमान 14 डिग्री और पंचकूला में 14.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. इसके विपरीत, नूंह में न्यूनतम तापमान 21.6 डिग्री और झज्जर में 20.7 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा. प्रदेश के औसत न्यूनतम तापमान में 0.5 डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की गई. मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार अगले कुछ दिनों में मौसम का मिजाज बदल सकता है.

कानपुर। सुबह और शाम कानपुर परिक्षेत्र में गुलाबी ठंडक होने लगी है। हिमालयी क्षेत्र से आ रहीं उत्तर पश्चिमी हवाओं की वजह से माहौल में नमी बनी हुई है। अधिकतम और न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य औसत से कम हैं। आने वाले दिनों में सुबह-शाम तापमान घटेगा। इधर, दशहरे पर हुई आतिशबाजी और पटाखों ने प्रदूषण बढ़ा दिया है। बृहस्पतिवार को शहर की हवा में प्रदूषण का स्तर 171 रहा। चिकित्सक इसे स्वास्थ्य के लिए हानिकारक बता रहे हैं।
चंद्रशेखर आजाद कृषि एवं प्रौद्योगिकी विवि के मौसम विभाग के नोडल एवं तकनीकी अधिकारी अजय मिश्रा ने बताया कि कड़ाके की ठंड तो अभी नहीं पड़ेगी लेकिन सुबह और शाम के समय हल्की गुलाबी ठंड अहसास होगा। गुरुवार को अधिकतम तापमान 32.2 और न्यूनतम तापमान 17 डिग्री रहा। अक्तूबर के अंत में यह केवल शुरुआती सर्दी है। खुले इलाकों में सुबह के समय हल्का धुंध या कोहरा भी देखने को मिल सकता है।

WMO Urges Early Humanitarian Action as El Niño Threatens Floods, Drought and Extreme Heat
Southeast Asia faces heat, rainfall shortages, wildfires and smoke hazards, and parts of western South America have already experienced severe flooding, as drought risks rise across parts of Central America, the southern Caribbean and the Amazon.
Humanitarian organizations need to prepare for an El Niño that could exceed the strength captured by monitoring charts used over the past four decades, according to the World Meteorological Organization's latest seasonal outlook, which projects a peak towards the end of the year and impacts lasting beyond it.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) have called for urgent, coordinated action before the worst effects arrive, drawing on weather, climate and water information to protect communities exposed to floods, drought and extreme heat.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said scientific forecasts and early warnings provide the means to save lives and protect livelihoods, stressing that a powerful El Niño does not have to become a humanitarian disaster if governments and aid organizations act decisively for the most vulnerable.
Regional forecasts reveal a narrowing window to prepare
The outlook issued on 21 October 2026 identifies heightened risks of heavy rainfall and flooding in parts of East Africa during the October–December rainy season, with drier conditions expected in Southern Africa from November threatening crops, water supplies and livelihoods.
Southeast Asia faces heat, rainfall shortages, wildfires and smoke hazards, and parts of western South America have already experienced severe flooding, as drought risks rise across parts of Central America, the southern Caribbean and the Amazon.
Extreme events are already occurring and are expected to multiply and trigger further disruptions as El Niño strengthens, placing additional pressure on refugees, displaced people and conflict-affected communities whose housing, water, sanitation and health services are already stretched.
Saulo warned that the opportunity to prepare remains open in many regions but will not last indefinitely, making early decisions essential to preventing dangerous weather from causing deaths and humanitarian emergencies. Seasonal outlooks describe regional tendencies rather than individual events, so humanitarian teams need national and regional forecasts, supported by expert interpretation, to determine where and when protective action is needed.
Turning weather information into humanitarian decisions
The WMO Coordination Mechanism (WCM), whose work featured at a side event during the fourth session of WMO's Commission for Weather, Climate, Hydrological, Marine and Related Environmental Services and Applications (SERCOM-4), helps humanitarian organizations translate forecasts into practical decisions.
As a core part of the Early Warnings for All initiative, WCM gathers authoritative information from WMO Members and Centres, provides timely expert advice for crisis-prone and conflict-affected regions, and develops tailored products with UN and humanitarian agencies to support preparedness, early action and response.
Its services include Global and Regional HydroMet Weekly scans, monthly climate briefings and scans, and capacity building for humanitarian staff, with previous support covering preparations for Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm Mocha in Myanmar and Bangladesh in 2023 and operations after Myanmar's 2025 earthquake.
Yi Wang, WMO's Chief of Severe Weather Services and WCM lead, said the mechanism has delivered more than 750 tailored products since 2022 and is now working with partners on El Niño preparedness, helping organizations turn reliable information into earlier action.
Opening the event, Véronique Bouchet, Senior Director of WMO's Department of Sciences, Services and Capacity Development, stressed that changing hazards hit displaced and crisis-affected communities hardest, making services designed around humanitarian planning and operational needs especially important.
SERCOM President Ian Lisk said information alone cannot ensure action, explaining that services must reflect how users make decisions and draw on the scientific expertise of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) and WMO Centres.
Wider participation and resources are needed
Marian Schilperoord, Deputy Director of UNHCR's Division of Emergency and Programme Support, and John Long, Head of OCHA's Emergency Response Preparedness Unit, emphasized stronger cooperation with WMO and the importance of national services and WMO Centres as trusted forecasting authorities.
Lisk called for more WMO Members to participate, continued user involvement and sufficient resources and capacity to expand WCM, encouraging national services to strengthen connections between authoritative forecasts, anticipatory action and crisis response.
Osvaldo Moraes, Chair of the Standing Committee on Disaster Risk Reduction and Early Warning Services, closed by stressing the need for adequate disaster risk reduction services, reinforcing the call for sustained investment and collaboration.
Around 50 participants attended the event, moderated by Marzia Santini, Chair of the Advisory Group on WCM and Lead of the European Crisis Management Laboratory at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, with a poster session bringing WCM staff, WMO Members and Centres, and humanitarian partners together to exchange experience across hazards and forecasting timescales.

Extreme heat is raising costs for local garment factories
As global temperatures rise, manufacturing and industrial sectors face a growing crisis: extreme heat. While global climate discussions often focus on emissions targets, the immediate challenge for Bangladesh’s $39 billion ready-made garment (RMG) industry lies inside its factories. The industry employs more than four million workers, and rising indoor temperatures are straining workers’ health, increasing operating costs and testing the industry’s ability to adapt.
The consequences of extreme heat are no longer abstract projections. Bangladesh lost an estimated 29 billion potential labour hours to heat exposure in 2024, a 92 percent increase on the 1990-99 average. This resulted in an estimated income loss of $24 billion, equivalent to nearly 5 percent of the country’s GDP.
Inside factories in Dhaka and Chattogram, conditions are becoming increasingly difficult. Indoor temperatures routinely exceed 35°C and can reach 40°C during peak summer months. A February survey by the Bangladesh Institute of Labour Studies (BILS) found that 78 percent of garment workers felt the summer heat had visibly worsened in recent years, with roughly half reporting weakness or illness as a direct result.
Keeping factory floors cool has become a business necessity rather than simply a matter of comfort. Factory managers are expanding the use of fans, improving ventilation and increasing maintenance of cooling systems. They are also ensuring access to safe drinking water and oral saline, introducing structured hydration breaks and first-aid protocols for heat-related illness, and adjusting working hours during severe heat spells.
These necessary measures come at a cost. Factory owners report that additional spending on electricity, backup generator fuel during power outages, drinking water and worker welfare programmes adds 2 to 5 percent to operating budgets during the peak summer months of April to June.
Extreme heat also directly affects productivity. A landmark 2025 study led by the University of Sydney and published in The Lancet Planetary Health, based on research inside Bangladeshi RMG factories, found that heat stress reduced output by 12 to 15 percent without cooling interventions, as workers slowed down under thermal strain. High temperatures cause fatigue, headaches and digestive illness, increasing error rates and production defects.
Poor sleep during hot nights and exhausting commutes leave workers arriving at factories already tired, contributing to absenteeism and health-related leave. However, the same study offered grounds for optimism. Targeted, low-cost interventions, such as cooling individual workers rather than entire factory floors, recovered a meaningful share of lost productivity. This suggests the problem can be addressed without prohibitive capital investment.
Factories cannot tackle the crisis alone. Workers’ living conditions determine how well they recover between shifts. Frequent power cuts, poor housing and inadequate water supplies in densely populated residential areas prevent workers from resting properly on hot nights, creating a cycle of fatigue. Building resilience requires targeted government investment in reliable electricity, clean water and climate-resilient urban infrastructure.
Global brands sourcing from Bangladesh must also recognise that suppliers cannot bear the costs of adaptation alone. Protecting supply chains requires long-term sourcing commitments, shared investment, realistic pricing that reflects rising operating costs, and the integration of climate resilience into core compliance frameworks. Without coordinated action, the next heatwave could become an industrial crisis.

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 23): The 2026/2027 Northeast Monsoon (MTL) is expected to begin on Oct 27 and continue until March next year, according to Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) director-general Dr Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip.
He said between three and five episodes of continuous heavy rain are expected to affect the country during the initial phase of the monsoon from November to January.
He said the situation could lead to flooding in low-lying areas and locations near rivers.
“Continuous strong northeasterly winds could also cause rough seas and rising sea levels in the South China Sea,” he said in a media statement on Friday.
As the monsoon enters its final phase, from January to March 2027, Mohd Hisham said rainfall was expected to decrease, particularly in the northern states of Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah.

The World Health Organization has warned that exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can increase the risk of complications. Here is how mothers can protect themselves and their babies.
Different parts of the world are experiencing high temperatures, including South Africa, where provinces such as Gauteng have been dealing with heatwaves.
While extreme heat can pose several health risks, it can also be dangerous for pregnant women and their unborn babies.
In a recent report, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that extreme heat can affect a child’s health even before birth.
"Heat exposure during pregnancy has been linked with preterm birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and other complications," states the organisation on X.
The organisation says "studies continue to provide evidence that exposure to extreme heat can harm health from pregnancy to childhood, leading to a 26% increase in the odds of preterm birth."
Exposure to heatwaves is also affecting newborn babies.
"Newborns are also increasingly exposed, with babies under one year of age experiencing 389% more heatwave days in 2024 compared with the 1986 to 2005 baseline period," reports the WHO.
It adds that 'globally, an estimated 1.5 billion children are exposed to heatwaves that are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe.'
With temperatures continuing to rise, protecting pregnant women and young children from extreme heat is becoming increasingly important.
Extreme heat can affect health before a child is even born. Heat exposure during pregnancy has been linked with preterm birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and other complications. Better monitoring can help health systems identify emerging risks - and protect women during and after pregnancy as well as their babies. Learn more: https://t.co/dMPYVsaj1y
— World Health Organization (WHO) (@WHO) October 22, 2026
The National Department of Health has highlighted that pregnant women, older persons, children, people living with chronic illnesses and other vulnerable groups need special attention during periods of extreme heat.
The department says they 'should take extra precautions to avoid overheating and dehydration, which can affect their health and well-being'.
Below are some of the ways women can take precautions during extreme heat weather conditions:
Stay hydrated:
Drink water regularly throughout the day. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should pay particular attention to their fluid intake.
Keep children cool:
Dress babies and children in lightweight clothing, keep them in cool, shaded or well-ventilated spaces, and never leave them unattended in parked vehicles.
Protect pregnant women:
Avoid strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest parts of the day, rest in cool places and drink water regularly. Seek medical advice if you feel unwell or experience signs of dehydration.
Avoid excessive heat exposure:
Limit outdoor activities during the hottest hours, usually from late morning to mid-afternoon. Where possible, schedule activities for cooler parts of the day.
Recognise warning signs:
Watch for dizziness, headaches, unusual weakness, nausea, excessive thirst or reduced urination. Confusion, fainting or very high body temperature may indicate a medical emergency and require immediate assistance.

Tamil Nadu orange alert conditions are expected across 17 districts on October 22, with the Chennai Regional Meteorological Centre warning of very heavy rain accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning. The alert follows the formation of a low-pressure area over the southwest Bay of Bengal and comes as heavy rain is forecast to continue in the state until October 26.
The districts under the orange alert are Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli, Kanniyakumari, Tenkasi, Virudhunagar, Ramanathapuram, Theni, Dindigul, Madurai, Coimbatore, Nilgiris, Sivaganga, Pudukkottai, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Mayiladuthurai. The warning was issued for rain of 11 to 20 centimetres within 24 hours.
V.R. Durai, director of the Chennai Regional Meteorological Centre, said the low-pressure area was influencing weather conditions over southern Tamil Nadu. The forecast covers several major urban and peri-urban areas, including Madurai and Coimbatore, as well as districts along the southern and Cauvery delta regions.
The alert also includes districts where intense rainfall can affect road movement, local drainage systems and access between urban centres and surrounding settlements. However, the source report does not provide specific forecasts of flooding, road closures, transport cancellations or municipal advisories for individual cities.
An additional set of districts has been placed under a forecast for heavy rain and thunderstorms. These are Tiruchirappalli, Erode, Ariyalur, Perambalur, Cuddalore, Namakkal, Viluppuram, Tiruppur and Karur, along with Puducherry. Chennai and its suburban areas are expected to remain cloudy, with moderate rain possible in isolated locations.
The weather office classifies rainfall of 6 to 11 centimetres as heavy rain and issues a yellow alert. Rainfall between 11 and 20 centimetres is classified under an orange alert, while precipitation above 20 centimetres attracts a red alert. These thresholds are used to communicate the expected intensity of rainfall and the level of preparedness required.
The forecast places southern Tamil Nadu and parts of the western and delta regions under heightened weather watch as the low-pressure system affects the state. The meteorological centre has said that heavy rain may persist through October 26, with the immediate orange alert applying to October 22.
